title: Building Mildam: open-ended AI suspects without letting dialogue rewrite the mystery
author: Select-Flounder-2593
selftext:
I'm the creator of Mildam, a Korean-language browser murder-mystery game. AI powers the suspect conversations, and AI tools also assisted development and artwork. I checked this post format with the moderators before sharing it.

The development decision I want to discuss is where to stop relying on generated dialogue. The mystery has authored facts, evidence and character motives, but players can ask suspects their own questions rather than choose from a fixed dialogue tree. Each character gets its own knowledge and goals, not an all-knowing view of every conversation.

I kept what a suspect says separate from what actually happens in the game. A promise to hand something over is not itself an inventory change, and a persuasive answer is not automatic proof that it is true. The game tracks evidence, permitted actions and the final outcome separately. That boundary lets characters conceal things or cooperate without treating every generated sentence as a new fact about the mystery. It is a design trade-off, not a claim that AI cannot make mistakes.

The screenshot is an actual lobby view from the game, not a concept mockup. Mildam is currently Korean-only. Guests can explore, collect evidence and reach an ending without logging in. Direct AI conversations require login and use credits. Signup and daily credits are provided; additional credits can be purchased, so the whole game is not free.

Game: [https://mildam.app](https://mildam.app)

For others building AI character games, where do you draw the boundary between a character's dialogue and authoritative game state?
